summary: We built a browser game in which players design, fly and evaluate a complete space mission under limited resources. You get only a goal — for example, "deliver 500 GB of Earth images within 12 months on a 450k budget" — and make every engineering decision yourself: orbit, launch vehicle, ground stations, and the spacecraft part by part. The mission launches only when your decisions pass every check. A simulation built on formulas from NASA documents then flies it day by day and explains across NASA's four mission segments (launch, space, ground, user) where and why it worked or failed. Six resources — mass, power, budget, data, communications and time — stay on screen the whole time, every part changes several of them, and many different designs can reach the same goal. This answers the challenge directly: students usually meet orbits, rockets and spacecraft as separate topics, and this game shows how the decisions pull on each other inside one mission — then lets you change one thing and fly again. Three missions, two difficulty levels, English and Ukrainian.
details:
What it does

KOSMOS turns the NASA mission life cycle into five stages:

  1. Goal — the need, the end product and the limits: budget, launch deadline, the NASA mass margin, and which role owns which decision.
  2. Concept — orbit, launch vehicle and ground stations (or the TDRS relay for the ISS mission), each with its consequences: orbital period, time in Earth's shadow, orbital lifetime, contact time with the ground.
  3. Design — build the spacecraft on a blueprint: bus, solar arrays, battery, radio, computer, attitude control, propulsion, and instruments or cargo. After every change six resources update — mass, power, budget, data, communications, time — and the checks are grouped by NASA's four mission segments.
  4. Flight — the server flies the whole mission and the game replays it in accelerated time on a flat Earth map: ground track, Earth's shadow, station visibility and contact sessions, battery, data, altitude, propellant and events. For the ISS mission a two-orbit view shows phasing, the Hohmann transfer and docking.
  5. Report — for each segment a cause-and-effect chain "your decision → physics with numbers → result", the bottleneck resource, four scores with their formulas (mission success, science value, resource efficiency, decision quality), a comparison with a similar real NASA mission, and with your previous attempt. From here you return to any stage and fly again.

Three missions: a training CubeSat released from the ISS (1 GB in 6 months, 150k budget, step-by-step hints); Satellite to orbit (500 GB of Earth images in 12 months, 450k); Cargo to the ISS (2,500 kg, at least 30% science, docking within 5 days, 1,500k). Each comes in a simple version, where the roles give advice, and an advanced version, where the roles state facts only, the player sets the part layout and the mass margin, and every resource opens a calculation sheet with the formula, the numbers and the NASA document it comes from.

The mission flies only on your decisions: "Launch mission" stays locked until every check passes, and the flight and the report open only for the design you launched.

Play together online. Up to four players join one mission over the internet, each taking a role — Planner, Scientist, Engineer or Designer. Every decision belongs to exactly one role, so the team has to negotiate: the Scientist's better camera eats the Engineer's power and the Planner's budget. Played alone, one player leads all four roles.

How it works

The backend (C#, ASP.NET Core on .NET 10, PostgreSQL) computes everything: orbit period and speed, J2 precession and sun-synchronous orbits, Earth's shadow and power balance, battery depth of discharge, ground contacts computed every 30 s above a 10° elevation mask, a link budget where the data rate falls with distance squared, atmospheric drag and orbital decay, the rocket equation, Hohmann transfer, plane change and ISS phasing, and NASA's 25-year disposal rule. Every formula and constant is traced to a NASA document with section and page; derived formulas and game estimates are labelled as such in the game. The frontend (React, TypeScript, MUI, i18next) only shows what the server computed. The same design and the same flight seed always give the same flight, so attempts — or a whole class's designs — can be compared fairly.

Benefits and intended impact

Students meet orbits, rockets and spacecraft as separate topics. KOSMOS lets high-school and university students (about 14–22) with no engineering background see the systems thinking of a mission team: every decision costs something elsewhere, there is no single right answer, and a failed design explains itself instead of just showing a score. It runs in any browser, with no sign-in and no installation, in English and Ukrainian.

How it is creative

  • Four roles — Planner, Scientist, Engineer and Designer — each own their decisions and comment on every change. Online, four players take one role each and must agree on one spacecraft; alone, the role comments make the same trade-offs visible.
  • Real NASA data inside the gameplay: parts from NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art 2026, ISS cargo from real resupply manifests, and a comparison of your design with 11 real NASA missions.
  • The report explains failure as a chain from your decision through physics to the result and names the one resource that limited the mission most.

Factors we considered

Honesty of numbers (every value shows its source: NASA, derived from NASA formulas, or game estimate), accessibility for beginners (two difficulty versions, a training mission with explained terms, two languages), fair comparison (deterministic seeds), teamwork (roles with single ownership so co-op players negotiate through shared resources, not shared buttons), and scope: in 48 hours we finished the full mission cycle before adding extras.

What we achieved and what comes next

Achieved: all three missions playable end to end on the live server, solo and online co-op for up to four players with one role each, both difficulty versions, physics with NASA sources, real NASA data in play, explanations and scores, two languages, original music, and automatic build, test and deploy.

Next steps — planned but not finished in 48 hours: reacting to events during the flight; resource graphs over time and "what to change" hints in the report; continents, the day–night line and 3D scenes in the flight view; personal goals for each role; more missions and an Arcade mode.

Tools

C#, ASP.NET Core (.NET 10), Entity Framework Core, PostgreSQL 17, xUnit; TypeScript, React 19, Vite, MUI, i18next, React Router; Docker; GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, Azure App Service and Azure Database for PostgreSQL; ffmpeg; DaVinci Resolve for the demo video; Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding and research assistant.
